name: Togo Kan
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress; 1 further work by the same author (or citing it for stress) agrees.
catalog_citation: Heath, Jeffrey. 2015. A Grammar of Togo Kan (Dogon language family, Mali). Ann Arbor: University of Michigan / Language Description Heritage Library (MPG PuRe, DOI 10.17617/2.2176494). xvi+445 pp.
catalog_locator: sec. 2.1.2 Prosody, p. 7; sec. 3.2.2 Metrical structure, p. 13; sec. 3.7 Tones, pp. 34-35; sec. 13.1 Focalization, p. 275
catalog_quote: 3.2.2 Metrical structure. If we assume that a shift to high vowels {i u} can reflect metrically weak positions in multisyllabic words, we can argue that the second and third of three syllables in a trisyllabic verb with final-syllable rhotic are weak in the bare stem (and related paradigmatic forms), but not in the imperative or some other verb forms. We can see this in alternations like túŋì-rⁿì ‘cause to kneel’ (bare stem) and its imperative túŋɔ́-rⁿɔ̀. For other trisyllabic verb stems (i.e. with a non-rhotic consonant in the final syllable), the second (but not third) syllable is weak even in the imperative, as in kúmúɲù ‘crumple’ (bare stem), imperative kúmúɲɔ́. [p. 13] ... Nearly all stems, nouns as well as verbs, have either /H/ (all-high) or /LH/ (rising) as the basic lexical melody. [p. 7] ... Syllables in TgK are H, L, <LH> (rising), <HL> (falling), and <LHL> (bell-shaped). [p. 35] ... Focalization is ordinarily not expressed by the form of the focalized constituent itself, except perhaps by extra prominence. [p. 275]
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: Togo Kan is described as a tone language (syllable tones H, L and three contours; lexical melodies /H/ and /LH/ with at least one H per stem; extensive grammatical tone overlays). No word-stress or accent is posited: the only metrical remark is that the second (and sometimes third) syllable of trisyllabic verb stems is 'metrically weak', inferred from vowel raising to i/u, i.e. weakness is medial/post-initial, which is compatible with an initial-syllable strong position but Heath does not say so.
new_statements.exceptions: None for stress; the metrical-weakness claim is limited to trisyllabic verb stems (rhotic-final vs other) and varies between bare stem and imperative.
new_statements.domain_note: Word/stem level (verb stems). The word 'stress' occurs only in the 2010/2011 drafts, sec. 13.1 Focalization (2010 p. 249): focus is 'ordinarily not expressed by the form of the focalized constituent itself, except perhaps by a little extra stress' -- phrase-level focal prominence, reworded to 'extra prominence' in the 2015 grammar (p. 275). Secs. 3.8 (pp. 57-58) and 2.1.2 (p. 7) cover intonation (final prolongation, 'dying-quail' pitch decline, clause-final tone-dropping/downdrift).
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog tene1248 [dtk] has no dialect children. Heath 2015 describes the Koporo-Pe dialect of Togo Kan (sec. 1.4.1, p. 5) and treats 'Tene Kan' (Toroli/Azanga area) as the same language (sec. 1.2, p. 1); Prost 1969 described the Pel dialect; Sagara & Andrason 2023 describe 'Teŋukan', the Dourou-community variety, which they call 'one of the dialects of Togo-Teŋukan' (p. 1). All fall under tene1248. The earlier scan's attribution of Heath 2015 to De Gruyter was not verified: the 2015 grammar on record is the Language Description Heritage / University of Michigan online publication (PuRe item_2176494).

new_statements.quote: Les tons sont haut (ɛ́ ɛ́ɛ́), bas (ɛ̀ ɛ̀ɛ̀), montant (ɛ̌ ɛ̀ɛ́), descendant (ɛ̂ ɛ́ɛ̀), et en forme de cloche (ɛ̌ɛ̀). Tous ces tons sauf le dernier peuvent se prononcer sur une syllabe courte CV contenant une voyelle courte. Nous plaçons l'accent tonal sur la voyelle, éventuellement aussi sur une consonne en fin de syllabe, surtout en cas de perte d'une voyelle finale et/ou lorsque la consonne représente un suffixe tonal: wǎǹ 'cuire' pour /wǎnù/, wı̀lé-m̀ 'faire pivoter' pour /wı̀lé-mù/. Comme dans les autres parlers dogon, les tons de base des mots (substantifs, verbes, etc.) sont sujets à des modifications apportées par le contexte morphosyntaxique.
new_statements.translation: The tones are high (ɛ́ ɛ́ɛ́), low (ɛ̀ ɛ̀ɛ̀), rising (ɛ̌ ɛ̀ɛ́), falling (ɛ̂ ɛ́ɛ̀), and bell-shaped (ɛ̌ɛ̀). All of these tones except the last can be pronounced on a short CV syllable containing a short vowel. We place the tone mark on the vowel, and possibly also on a syllable-final consonant, especially where a final vowel has been lost and/or where the consonant represents a tonal suffix: wǎǹ 'cook' for /wǎnù/, wı̀lé-m̀ 'make pivot' for /wı̀lé-mù/. As in the other Dogon languages, the base tones of words (nouns, verbs, etc.) are subject to modifications brought about by the morphosyntactic context.

new_statements.relation_note: Same reading as the existing statement from Heath 2015 (tone language, no stress statement); adds nothing on stress. Same variety: the co-author/consultant Boukel Togo is 'ressortissant de Koporo-Pen', the Koporo-Pe dialect described in the 2015 grammar. Whole-word a full-text search for stress/accent/prominence/intonation across the 142 pp. hits only 'l'accent tonal' in the preface; 'ton' elsewhere is only the French possessive.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The lexique treats Togo Kan as a tone language (H, L, rising, falling, bell-shaped tones marked on every entry, base tones altered by morphosyntactic context) and says nothing about word stress; 'accent tonal' in the preface means the tone diacritic, not stress.
new_statements.exceptions: none (no stress statement to have exceptions)
new_statements.identity_note: The lexique's consultant Boukel Togo is from Koporo-Pen, i.e. the Koporo-Pe dialect of Togo Kan that Heath's 2015 grammar describes (sec. 1.4.1, p. 5); the Living Tongues sketch held by the project describes the Teŋukan variety of Dourou. Prost 1969 (Pel dialect, Dakar, 164 pp.) remains not obtained; no digital copy located.

tone_statements.quote: 2 tone levels: other Songhay languages, all Dogon languages [...] I refer to this type of tonation as the “dying quail” effect (symbol \). It is associated with certain constructions that normally combine two parallel phrases. In Jamsay and Togo Kan, dying quail is regular in NP conjunction (‘X and Y’). [...] The data show that the compromise pattern is most common for Jamsay, but prioritization of tonosyntax is typical for Togo Kan.

Typology discussion piece, 'Typological and historical topics for Dogon', Dogon and Bangime Linguistics (Moran, Steven & Forkel, Robert & Heath, Jeffrey, eds.), dogonlanguages.info. 7 pp.
tone_statements.quote: Most Dogon languages have a constraint on noun, verb, adjective, and numeral stems against all-low lexical tone melodies. [...] For example, the lexically /LH/-toned Togo Kan noun gìrⁿí ‘house’ is overlaid with {L} before an adjective (1a) and with {H} (reduced for a bimoraic noun from the full form {HL}) after a possessor (1b). If we combine N-Adj and Poss-N into Poss-N-Adj, we see that the possessor trumps the adjective. In fact, the adjective is included in the possessor-controlled{HL} overlay.

tone.says: Classes all Dogon languages as having two tone levels H and L (vs 3 in Bangime/Bozo/Jalkunan/Tiefo, pitch accent in Tamashek, none in Fulfulde etc.); describes melodies, overlays, sandhi, floating tones, tonosyntax; for Togo Kan: dying-quail tonation is regular in NP conjunction and, when a conjoined NP is a tonosyntactic target, Togo Kan typically prioritises the {L} overlay over the tonation (Jamsay compromises).

sources.quote: Most Dogon languages have a constraint on noun, verb, adjective, and numeral stems against all-low lexical tone melodies. [...] For example, the lexically /LH/-toned Togo Kan noun gìrⁿí ‘house’ is overlaid with {L} before an adjective (1a) and with {H} (reduced for a bimoraic noun from the full form {HL}) after a possessor (1b). If we combine N-Adj and Poss-N into Poss-N-Adj, we see that the possessor trumps the adjective. In fact, the adjective is included in the possessor-controlled{HL} overlay.

tone.quote: For a few verbs, the 2sg imperative inflection is encoded by means of tone alone: gàrá ‘go past’ versus gárá ‘go past!’. … the nominal root siɲe ‘noise’ and the verb dagu ‘cease/stop!’ which is additionally marked by the 2sg imperative suffix and tonal pattern and surfaces as dàgà … propose that summonses tend to contain high and/or front vowels (i.e., I- or U-type) and bear high tones … TTKD data do not support it (note the use of E and O type vowels and the common presence of low tone).
